title: Meeting Room & Calendar Scheduler — LLD
summary: A harder version of "check one resource for overlap": finding a slot free for a room and every attendee at once, plus recurrence expanded without materializing years of instances.

slides.markdown:
"Design a meeting room booking system" sounds like it reduces to checking one room's calendar for overlaps — and if you scope it that way, you'll finish the interview early having solved the easy 20% of the problem.

The real system has to satisfy **every attendee's calendar** simultaneously, not just the room's, and handle recurring meetings (a weekly standup) without pre-generating years of individual occurrences. Those two requirements are where the actual design work lives.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: what's in scope, what isn't
slides.markdown:
**In scope:** rooms with a capacity and a booking calendar; meetings with a list of attendees, a time range, and optionally a recurrence rule; conflict detection across a room and all its attendees; rescheduling and cancellation.

**Explicitly out of scope:** video-call platform integration (Zoom/Meet links) and room hardware/IoT concerns — treat a room purely as a bookable time-and-capacity resource.

Framing this early as "multi-resource conflict detection," not "one room's calendar," sets the right scope before you start drawing classes.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Room, Meeting, Attendee, RecurrenceRule, Calendar
slides.markdown:
`Calendar` is the reusable abstraction here — both a `Room` and an `Attendee` have one, and both are checked the same way. A `Meeting` references a room, a list of attendees, a time range, and optionally a `RecurrenceRule` describing how it repeats.

Critically, a recurring `Meeting` is stored once, as a rule ("every Monday 10am"), not as N pre-generated occurrence rows — `RecurrenceRule` is a separate value object precisely so expansion into concrete instances can happen on demand rather than at creation time.

Giving `Room` and `Attendee` the same `Calendar` interface is what lets conflict-checking code treat "is this room free" and "is this person free" as the same operation, just applied to different resources.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: checking one resource for a conflict
The hard part: a slot free for the room AND every attendee
slides.markdown:
Booking a meeting isn't "is the room free" — it's "is the room free, and is every one of the N attendees free, all at the same proposed time." Checking these one at a time and rejecting on the first conflict works for validation, but it doesn't help you find a **free** slot; it only tells you a specific guess failed.

To actually find a free slot, you need the intersection of free/busy across all N+1 calendars (the room plus each attendee) — a time is only usable if it's free in every single one. With 10 attendees, that's 11 calendars whose free intervals must overlap.

The efficient approach: pull each calendar's busy intervals for the search window, merge each into sorted non-overlapping busy blocks, then walk all N+1 sorted interval lists together to find gaps common to all of them — rather than testing candidate time slots one at a time against every calendar.

![Four stacked timelines for Room and three Attendees, with the narrow common free slot highlighted](assets/common-free-slot.svg)

Seeing all four timelines stacked makes it visual why a slot has to be free in every row at once — the common free slot is often much narrower than any single row's free time would suggest.

assets.alt: Four stacked timelines for Room and three Attendees, with the narrow common free slot highlighted

slides.sectionTitle: Code: expanding a recurrence rule lazily
Compare: eager materialization vs lazy expansion of recurring instances
slides.markdown:
| | Eager materialization | Lazy expansion |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | One row per occurrence, grows without bound over time | One row per rule, regardless of how long it runs |
| Query cost | Simple — just read existing rows | Computed on demand from the rule for the queried window |
| Editing "this and future" occurrences | Requires bulk-updating many rows | Split the rule at that date — cheap, one new rule |
| Handling exceptions (one occurrence moved/cancelled) | Natural — that row is just edited | Needs a separate exceptions list layered on the rule |

**How to decide:** lazy expansion wins for pure storage and edit-going-forward efficiency, but real calendar apps (Google Calendar included) end up needing an exceptions list anyway for one-off changes — so the practical answer is lazy expansion plus a small exceptions table, not either extreme alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending to double-booking policies per room type
slides.markdown:
Not every room needs the same conflict-handling strictness. A dedicated executive boardroom should hard-block any conflicting booking, while a large open-plan huddle space might allow a soft double-booking with a warning, since two small groups sometimes genuinely fit.

Modeling this as a `DoubleBookingPolicy` on `Room` (`HardBlockPolicy` vs `AllowWithWarningPolicy`) keeps the conflict-check logic itself unchanged — `hasConflict` still runs the same way, but what the system *does* with a true result (reject outright vs. warn and allow) is delegated to the room's policy.

This is a smaller, more targeted use of the same plug-in-a-policy shape seen elsewhere in this group's pricing strategies — proof that the pattern generalizes beyond pricing.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: checking conflicts only at creation time
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Conflict detection runs when a meeting is created — once it's booked, it's booked, no further checks needed."

**Why it's wrong:** meetings get rescheduled constantly, and a reschedule is really a delete-and-recreate at a new time. If the system only validates conflicts at creation and treats a reschedule as a special "just update the time" path that skips the same check, it silently introduces double-bookings that creation-time validation would have caught.

**Correct model:** every operation that changes a meeting's time or attendee list — creation, reschedule, or adding an attendee after the fact — must run through the same conflict-check path, not a shortcut that assumes an already-valid meeting stays valid after being edited.
